(a) Design Requirements.—
        (1) In general.—The design of the coins minted under this Act shall be emblematic of the fight against breast cancer. 
        (2) Designation and inscriptions.—On each coin minted under this Act there shall be—
            (A) a designation of the face value of the coin; 
            (B) an inscription of the year “2018”; and 
            (C) inscriptions of the words “Liberty”, “In God We Trust”, “United States of America”, and “E Pluribus Unum”.   
    (b) Selection.—The design for the coins minted under this Act shall be selected by the Secretary based on the winning design from a juried, compensated design competition described under subsection (c). 
    (c) Design Competition.—
        (1) In general.—The Secretary shall hold a competition and provide compensation for its winner to design the obverse and reverse of the coins minted under this Act. The competition shall be judged by an expert jury chaired by the Secretary and consisting of three members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee who shall be elected by such Committee and three members from the Commission of Fine Arts who shall be elected by such Commission. 
        (2) Proposals.—As part of the competition described in this subsection, the Secretary may accept proposals from artists, engravers of the United States Mint, and members of the general public, and any designs submitted for the design review process described herein shall be anonymized until a final selection is made. 
        (3) Accompanying designs; preference for physical designs.—The Secretary shall encourage three-dimensional designs to be submitted as part of the proposals, and the jury shall give a preference for proposals that are accompanied by a three-dimensional physical design instead of, or in addition to, an electronic design. 
        (4) Compensation.—The Secretary shall determine compensation for the winning design under this subsection, which shall be not less than $5,000. The Secretary shall take into account this compensation amount when determining the sale price described in section 6(a).

fable.w: The Secretary must select the coin design based on the winner of a competition judged by an expert jury that includes members of the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, an advisory body of citizen and expert members, so outsiders take part in a federal decision. The tempting "No" reading treats this as an internal Treasury process, or treats the design submissions as mere applications for a prize. That reading fails because the jury brings advisory committee members into the selection itself, and the general public may also submit proposals.
fable.s: The competition shall be judged by an expert jury chaired by the Secretary and consisting of three members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee who shall be elected by such Committee and three members from the Commission of Fine Arts who shall be elected by such Commission.

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Secretary to select a coin design based on the judgment of an expert jury. This jury includes members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee and the Commission of Fine Arts, which are advisory bodies composed of non-federal experts and public representatives. Their role in judging the competition constitutes participation by outside parties in a federal decision.
qwen_block.s: The competition shall be judged by an expert jury chaired by the Secretary and consisting of three members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee who shall be elected by such Committee and three members from the Commission of Fine Arts who shall be elected by such Commission.

opus.w: The Secretary must select the coin design based on the winner picked by an expert jury that includes three members elected by the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee. That committee is an advisory body made up largely of outside citizens, so non-federal people take part in a federal decision. The jury being chaired by the Secretary, and partly drawn from the Commission of Fine Arts, does not remove that outside involvement. The section also lets members of the general public submit design proposals.
opus.s: The design for the coins minted under this Act shall be selected by the Secretary based on the winning design from a juried, compensated design competition described under subsection (c).
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading, and why it fails.** It is tempting to say "No" on two grounds: the jury is chaired by the Secretary, and the Commission of Fine Arts is a federal body. Neither works against the definition. The Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee is an advisory committee made up mostly of outside citizens who represent the public. The Secretary must pick the coin design based on the winner chosen by this jury, so outside members help make a federal decision, just as the advisory board did in Example 10. The public can also submit designs. That is a contest entry, not an application for a benefit.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary to select a coin design based on a competition judged by a jury that includes members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee and the Commission of Fine Arts. These committees are composed of private citizens and experts outside the federal government, constituting an advisory panel with non-federal members involved in the decision. Additionally, the competition is open to the general public, allowing them to participate in the design selection process.
qwen_chat.s: The competition shall be judged by an expert jury chaired by the Secretary and consisting of three members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee who shall be elected by such Committee and three members from the Commission of Fine Arts who shall be elected by such Commission.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "juried, compensated design competition" is merely an application process (like applying for a grant or contract), which the definition explicitly excludes. However, the definition states that participation includes public hearings, meetings, or advisory bodies, and a competition open to the "general public" where designs are judged by a committee involving outside experts (Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, Commission of Fine Arts) constitutes a form of public participation in the decision-making process regarding the coin's design. The key is that the general public is invited to submit proposals, and the selection involves a jury with non-federal members (the CCAC and CFA are typically composed of private citizens/experts, not federal employees).

Wait, let's look closer at the definition. "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." Is a design competition an application for a benefit? It's a competition for a contract/award. But the definition also says: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." And "It might also be a comment period, public hearing, or public meeting." A design competition open to the general public is a mechanism for the public to participate in the decision of what the coin looks like. Furthermore, the jury includes members from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee and the Commission of Fine Arts. These are advisory committees composed of private citizens (outside the federal government). The definition says: "an advisory committee, board, or panel that includes non-federal members... is Yes." The jury is a panel that includes non-federal members.

Therefore, the label is Yes.
